description: Chess with four wolves that belong to neither player, and a price on their heads. Each wolf walks its own five-square loop on a wing, stepping on after every move either player makes and eating whatever piece it lands on; no king may stand where one will step next. Only a knight can take a wolf, and each one earns its taker a point. Checkmate still wins, but a game that reaches the move limit or goes too long without progress goes to the player with more points. The point turns a hazard into a quarry: without it, wolves like these are something to go round and nearly every game ends with one still walking; with it, the computer players hunt them from the opening, take about three times as many, and two games in five end with the board cleared. The cost is a knight's time, spent on a point that counts only if nobody is mated first.
name: wolf hunt

provenance.history: Hand-written as archive/wolves.json plus scoring.count "points" and a bounty of 1 on both routes, against a wolf of value 3 (Q76). A one-key experiment on what a bounty does to play, against a control already measured; rows 19 and 22 of reference/schema-showcase-coverage.md.
